items.title: In 1992, Annie Lennox blew David Bowie away while rehearsing ‘Under Pressure’ for Freddie Mercury tribute
items.summary:
Rock fans around the world were still in mourning. A mere five months after the death of  Queen  frontman Freddie Mercury, his bandmates gathered some of the biggest names in music for a  concert  at London’s Wembley Stadium. It was unlike anything since  Live Aid .  The Freddie Mercury Tribute Concert  began as a fond farewell to  one of rock’s greatest legends . Over the course of the night, it became a global call for compassion and action in the fight against HIV/AIDS.

Photo credit: “ Freddie Mercury ” by kentarotakizawa is licensed under CC BY 2.0 . – Fans are thrilled to hear Freddie Mercury's iconic voice once again. 

Globally, the concert reached an estimated audience of about a billion people. Onstage, rock stars from Metallica and  Elton John  to George Michael and Guns N’ Roses paid homage to Mercury and the songs he crafted with Queen. When  David Bowie  stepped onstage to perform “Under Pressure,” the audience knew something special was about to happen. What they did not know was who would take on the challenge of performing Mercury’s half of the song. 

A rehearsal that revealed something extraordinary 

In 1981, “Under Pressure” reached the #1 spot on the singles charts in over 10 countries. It was Queen’s second-ever #1 single in the UK, and, for Bowie, his third UK #1 at that point. Mercury’s vocals carry enormous emotional weight and replacing him was understandably intimidating. Enter an unexpected choice: former Eurythmics lead singer Annie Lennox.

In rehearsal footage that has circulated online for years, you can see for yourself just how nervous…
items.t: In 1992, Annie Lennox blew David Bowie away while rehearsing ‘Under Pressure’ for Freddie Mercury tribute

items.title: 4 everyday phrases that may indicate someone is highly intelligent
items.summary:
So often, we equate intelligence with standardized testing , degrees or rank in a graduating class. The person who has a 4.0 GPA and a high SAT score is probably pretty book-smart. And sure, having several degrees does imply that someone has likely had a lot of education.

But there is another measure of intelligence that is often overlooked : the ability to be wrong. Emma Jones , MD, a self-described hospice doctor and “burnout coach,” went viral on social media in fall 2025 for a video in which she talks about intelligence. The clip is titled “Here’s how you know someone is highly intelligent.” In just a couple of minutes, she lays out ways you can easily spot someone who is ultra-bright.

View this post on Instagram 

Quoting Oscar Wilde , she says, “Consistency is the last refuge of the unimaginative.” The comments, and there are thousands of them, support the notion.

The phrases smart people actually use 

Here’s where the phrases of (most likely) highly intelligent people come in. She says to listen for sentences like:

“I used to think…”

“That’s a good point.”

“Let me reconsider.”

“I’ve changed my mind.”

She adds, “Most people double down to protect their ego. But intelligent people update their beliefs. They get more curious instead of more defensive . And they ask things like ‘what am I missing?’ instead of trying to win an argument. They don’t tie their identity to being ‘right.’ And they treat being wrong like data, not humiliation.”

She also cites a popular quote often attributed to Albert Einstein: “The measure of intelligence is the ability to change”…
items.t: 4 everyday phrases that may indicate someone is highly intelligent

items.title: It took 343 embroiderers in 46 countries 13 years to make one absolutely stunning dress
items.summary:
Few things bring people together more beautifully than art. Whether it’s music, sculpture, paint or fabric , the arts are a way for us to express ourselves , our cultures and our common humanity.

But rarely do we witness one singular piece of art truly encapsulating the creativity of our human family.

At first glance, the dress created for the Red Dress project is quite obviously stunning. It looks as though it could be worn by a royal, though a royal from where? The style, colors and patterns of the dress don’t shout any particular country or culture; in fact, we can point to different elements of it and say it looks like it belongs on any continent.

One dress, 51 countries, 14 years in the making 

There’s a reason for that. The dress is made out of 87 pieces of burgundy silk dupion, which spent 14 years being sent around the world to be embroidered by 380 people from 51 countries: a truly global, multicultural creation.

Of those 380 embroiderers, 141 were commissioned artisans who were paid for their work and receive a portion of all ongoing exhibition fees. The rest were volunteers who contributed their stitches at events in various countries. The vast majority of embroiderers were women; approximately 97% identified as female.

British textile artist Kirstie Macleod conceived the project in 2009 as “an investigation into identity, with a desire to connect with women from around the world without borders and boundaries.” The basic design started as a sketch on the back of a napkin and has grown into a tangible garment that is not only a gorgeous work of art but a…
items.t: It took 343 embroiderers in 46 countries 13 years to make one absolutely stunning dress

items.title: Kindergarteners in 1949 were asked to draw their dads from memory. The results are stunning.
items.summary:
It was just another day in West Hartford, Connecticut. The year was 1949 and the place was Sedgwick Elementary School. Father’s Night was approaching, so kindergarten teacher Doris Morcom asked her young students to draw portraits of their dads . From the Inside History (via @Life) Instagram description, “Each child drew a portrait of their father entirely from memory.”

View this post on Instagram 

A visit from Life Magazine 

What made this extra special was that Al Fenn , a photographer from Life Magazine, was there to photograph the children with their fathers holding up the drawings. The photos revealed “portraits that were both delightfully imperfect and surprisingly accurate, offering a tender glimpse in the way children see their parents.”

Fenn, incidentally, spent 15 years at Life Magazine, creating some diverse, iconic photos. The Life website shares, “In 1931, as a gift on his first visit to Europe, Al Fenn (1912-1995) was given a Leica . By the time he returned to the States, his ‘heart now belonged to photography.'”

View this post on Instagram 

What the internet had to say 

In each picture, the children seemed to beam while their fathers looked, by contrast, somewhat serious. These photos have been posted on many social media sites, but on the Inside History reel, many of the commenters mention how business-like the fathers looked in their suits. One writes, “Not ONE dad looks happy from the results.” But this gets some pushback from, well, a middle aged man. “They are happy. This is how middle aged white dudes look when we’re happy. I feel so…
items.t: Kindergarteners in 1949 were asked to draw their dads from memory. The results are stunning.

items.title: Conflict experts share the 1 phrase to stop an argument before things get out of control
items.summary:
Has getting into a heated argument with your significant other, a coworker, or a child ever solved anything? Probably not. Heated arguments often lead people down the dark path of personal attacks, animosity, and so much agitation that they stop making sense altogether. However, conflict is a natural and healthy part of our daily lives, so disagreements can be very productive when we know how to handle them.

“If no one ever argues, you’re not likely to give up on old ways of doing things, let alone try new ones. Disagreement is the antidote to groupthink,” organizational psychologist Adam Grant said, according to Psychology Today . “We’re at our most imaginative when we’re out of sync.” So the big question is: How do we prevent heated arguments from happening and steer them to more productive territory instead?

Coworkers having an argument. Photo credit: Canva 

How to stop an argument from happening 

A group of researchers at the University of Wisconsin found that it’s essential for people to create a safe environment for discussion, and the key to doing so is to ask open-ended questions that lead to points of agreement. Specifically, the researchers say to use “I” statements, such as “I feel frustrated” or “I feel concerned,” when expressing yourself during the disagreement. However, the most effective phrase is one that clearly directs the discussion toward agreement.

The best way to stop an argument is with the phrase: “I’d actually like to focus on all the things we agree on.”

Coworkers come to an agreement. Photo credit: Canva 

There are three big reasons why…
items.t: Conflict experts share the 1 phrase to stop an argument before things get out of control

items.title: If you struggle with changing people’s minds, it probably says something positive about you
items.summary:
If you ever had a hard time persuading someone to change their mind , whether it’s a work decision, a disagreement with a child, or trying to get grandma to change her cable subscription, it can be frustrating. It can even make you doubt your knowledge on a subject—even if you know it well—because you couldn’t explain it to someone else.

The funny thing is that if you can’t explain something you are well-versed in to someone with half the understanding, it’s probably because you’re highly intelligent. Research has found repeatedly that experts in a subject are often pretty bad at explaining it to others because they can’t bridge the gap between their knowledge and the other person’s.

The curse of knowledge 

The problem is that if you have a hard time persuading people to change their minds, you may think you aren’t the expert that you thought you were. However, psychology experts say the exact opposite, and they have a dramatic name for the problem: the curse of knowledge.

A frustrated teacher. Credit: Canva 

“Lots of us have expertise in particular areas. Becoming an expert in something means that we become more and more fascinated by nuance and complexity,” Chip and Dan Heath write in Stick: Why Some Ideas Survive and Others Die. “That’s when the curse of knowledge kicks in, and we start to forget what it’s like not to know what we know.”

The curse of knowledge stems from people’s natural inclination to forget what they knew before they became experts. That’s why it can be hard for a parent in their 40s to explain basic math to a 9-year-old. 

“That is the curse of…
items.t: If you struggle with changing people’s minds, it probably says something positive about you

items.title: A drum sound on ‘Stayin’ Alive’ repeats for a reason you can hear in another Bee Gees hit
items.summary:
From the opening beat, the Bee Gees’ 1977 hit “Stayin’ Alive” has one of the most recognizable sounds in disco history. But the secret behind its steady rhythm lies in another of their hits, “Night Fever.” When the band’s drummer had to leave a recording session, the musicians came up with a creative solution that helped give the song its distinctive sound .

What began as a quick fix became the signature beat of “ Stayin’ Alive .” And it all happened long before musicians could copy and repeat a recording on a computer.

The Bee Gees needed a drummer. They found another solution. 

The Bee Gees were working on songs for the soundtrack to Saturday Night Fever , the film starring John Travolta. Recording sessions were underway at Le Château Studios, about an hour north of Paris, France, when their drummer, Dennis Bryon, had to return to England for a family matter.

The filmmakers were waiting to hear “Stayin’ Alive,” and finding a replacement drummer on short notice wasn’t easy. Recording engineer Karl Richardson described the problem in a 2000 interview with Mix .

The group first tried using an electric organ’s built-in drum machine, but the results were disappointing.

“It sounded terrible,” Richardson said.

Producer Albhy Galuten had an idea, which he described in a 2002 interview with Berklee College of Music .

“Back then, drum machines were really primitive, not even close to what they are today. I had a brainstorm and told Karl we should take a bar from ‘Night Fever,’ which we had already recorded, and make a drum loop,” said Galuten.

Two bars of music become a…
items.t: A drum sound on ‘Stayin’ Alive’ repeats for a reason you can hear in another Bee Gees hit

items.title: The Beatles threw the Monkees a party. Micky Dolenz hid the guests in a song.
items.summary:
Monkees vocalist Micky Dolenz was in London in 1967 when the band found themselves at the kind of party that could only have happened in the Swinging Sixties.

As a farewell celebration following the group’s London shows, a private gathering was held at the Speakeasy. This already famous club was a popular after-hours haunt for London’s music-industry crowd. Music manager Vic Lewis organized the July 3 party, and John Lennon, Paul McCartney and George Harrison were among the guests , along with Eric Clapton, The Who, Manfred Mann and Dusty Springfield.

Dolenz would later reveal the experience inspired a song he wrote afterward, which became his first commercially released composition for The Monkees.

Some accounts place the songwriting during an earlier part of the London visit. So the precise chronology is a bit murkier than the legend makes it sound. But what isn’t murky is what Dolenz did with those wild experiences and larger-than-life characters he encountered, which went on to shape a tune named “Randy Scouse Git.”

The Beatles are hiding in the lyrics 

The song’s most conspicuous clue is the line about “the four kings of E.M.I.” 

Those four kings were, of course, The Beatles, who were signed to EMI. Dolenz later explained that the line referred to the band and their recently released Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band . This album arrived just weeks before his London adventures.

The lyrics contain a few more clues about the people around Dolenz at the time. 

“The being known as Wonder Girl” referred to Samantha Juste, whom Dolenz had fallen for and would…
items.t: The Beatles threw the Monkees a party. Micky Dolenz hid the guests in a song.

items.title: A crash closed the highway an hour before their wedding. An elk hunter saved the day with his dirt bike.
items.summary:
Erich Thalacker and Kyla Dickey wanted their wedding photos to feel big. So on their wedding day , they drove up into Idaho’s Sawtooth Mountains in their suit and dress for a photo shoot before heading back to the ceremony at South Fork Lodge in Lowman .

“We wanted to capture that, and we wanted to feel wild and adventurous and whatnot,” Thalacker told KTVB, according to Yahoo! .

On the way back, they got more adventure than they’d planned. A fatal crash had closed Highway 21, cutting them off from the lodge, 16 miles away. The estimated wait was four hours, which was bad since the ceremony was in one.

“My jaw dropped a little bit,” Dickey said. “Like, oh my, I don’t even know what we can do to get around this.”

Also stuck in the backup was Garrett Kerr, who was heading home to Eagle after 10 days elk hunting, with a large elk in the back of his pickup. He’d seen helicopters overhead and guessed the road was in trouble. Then a man in a three-piece suit walked up to his truck and asked how long the closure would last, explaining he had to get to his wedding in an hour.

“I’m going to get you to your wedding,” Kerr told him.

Kerr had a small electric pit bike he’d used to haul the elk out of the woods. He also found a woman named Jessica who had an ATV. So Dickey climbed onto the ATV, Thalacker got on the back of the pit bike, a vehicle he’d never ridden before and that wasn’t built for two, and the little convoy worked its way around the crash and down the 16 miles to the lodge.

Representative image of a bride in her wedding dress walking toward a man on a dirt bike.…
items.t: A crash closed the highway an hour before their wedding. An elk hunter saved the day with his dirt bike.

items.title: Therapist explains why so many of us always feel ‘drained’ using a powerful ‘fire hose’ metaphor
items.summary:
So often when we open our phones or laptops, we are bombarded by content from platforms to which we didn’t even subscribe. For some, it’s becoming more and more difficult to weed out all the “noise.” And yet, now more than ever, we need to find ways to do that in order to de-stress .

Therapist Kier Gaines discusses this notion on a recent episode of the Mel Robbins Podcast . With a chyron reading “This is why you feel drained all the time,” he explains how the world seems to operate, at least in terms of getting people hooked on social media/television. He shares, “The world isn’t really designed to support your peace and happiness.”

View this post on Instagram 

How the world is designed 

Instead, Gaines shares, “The world is designed for your productivity and for your attention. And that’s it. If you just take a look at where we spend the majority of our time…social media, watching the news, being subject to marketing.”

He then asks how that makes us feel. “What are they designed to do? Social media is designed to make you feel like you’re behind. Marketing is designed to make you feel like you’re being left out. The news is designed…I don’t know what the news was originally designed for, but now it’s designed to scare the hell out of you.”

He explains just how pervasive it is. “When you open up your social media feed, you are being subjected to tens of millions of bad takes and half-chewed ideas, unsolicited and without your consent. And it’s like you’re drinking from a fire hose. If you drink from a water fountain, it quenches your thirst. If you drink from a fire…
items.t: Therapist explains why so many of us always feel ‘drained’ using a powerful ‘fire hose’ metaphor

items.title: Montreal Is Harnessing Soothing Ocean Sounds to Combat Traffic Noise
items.summary:
P arc des Madelinots, a humble wedge of green space in the Verdun borough of Montreal, is not in the most tranquil of settings. The 6,500-square-foot pocket park sits beside a busy junction and is flanked on two sides by roads often filled with cars. 

For years, locals in the historically working-class neighborhood had to deal with the noise of constant passing vehicle traffic while trying to relax, meet with friends, play with their kids or, indeed, do anything else in this outdoor community space.  

But today, Parc des Madelinots is bathed in a very different kind of sound: the lap of ocean waves, dulcet bird calls and the crunch of sand underfoot. 

Reasons to Be Cheerful · Parc des Madelinots Soundscape 
 It’s not because a beach has suddenly arrived in Verdun. The sounds are recordings being broadcast in an attempt to reshape urban noise, fighting sound with sound in a constructive way to reduce noise-induced disturbance, reinvigorate the use of the public space and even preserve cultural memory for displaced communities. 

“Sound is more than just noise, it can be a powerful resource,” says Catherine Guastavino, a professor at McGill University and principal investigator of Sounds in the City , a research team that is one of the collaborators on Les Madelinéennes , the sonic project in Parc des Madelinots. “We can use sounds to improve people’s experience of places.” 

A field recording session at the Parc des Madelinots. Credit: Paysages

items.t: Montreal Is Harnessing Soothing Ocean Sounds to Combat Traffic Noise

items.title: The Waterless, Hyper-Efficient Machines That Clean Clothes With Carbon Dioxide
items.summary:
This story was originally published by Grist . Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here . 

Doing the laundry has grown easier and more efficient over the years, yet two things have always remained the same: A washing machine needs water, and a dryer needs heat. Technology designed to clean aerospace parts reimagines the process by ditching both of those in favor of an unlikely substitute: carbon dioxide, the very gas we’re trying so hard to contain.

Under pressure, CO2 becomes a low-viscosity liquid capable of penetrating fabrics and carrying away oils and grime. When depressurized, it reverts to a gas, leaving clothes clean and dry. No wastewater. No dryer.

Beyond its novelty, the idea could clean up a resource-intensive chore. The average family runs roughly 300 loads a year, consuming thousands of gallons of water. And more than 80 percent of U.S. households own a dryer, with one study putting the annual CO2 emissions from machine drying alone at 27 million metric tons .

Tersus Solutions’ industrial CO2 washers use high pressure to turn carbon dioxide into a liquid that can clean fabrics without water. The machines’ bulky pressure chambers, pumps, pipes and compressors illustrate the challenge appliance makers face in trying to shrink the technology for household use. Courtesy of Teresus Solutions 
 Long confined to industrial operations, liquid-CO2 cleaning is getting a second look from appliance giants LG and Samsung — this time for the home. Still, shrinking a technology built around bulky, high-pressure machinery to fit both a laundry room and household budget…
items.t: The Waterless, Hyper-Efficient Machines That Clean Clothes With Carbon Dioxide

items.title: What We’re Reading: Phone Bans Are Improving Kids’ Test Scores
items.summary:
Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. 

Get smart 
 Over the last decade, the rise of smartphones across the U.S. has coincided with a significant drop in kids’ performance at school. Now, as the New York Times reports in a story shared by Executive Editor Will Doig, a new study has found that school phone bans are leading to modest improvements. Published this week by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard, the study included 3.3 million students in third through tenth grade, comparing the math and reading test scores of students at schools with and without strict phone bans.  

Though the gains seen at the schools with phone bans were modest, they suggest that gradual improvement is underway. 

Will says: 
 As a parent, there are so many reasons I’m in favor of banning phones at school, academics being just one of them. Still, it’s great to see data showing proof of concept on that aspect. 

Mapping roots 

In other phone-related news, there’s now an app that can help you find remarkable old trees. According to a Guardian article shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, Ancient Trees offers a curated map of notable trees. 

“I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing,” the app’s creator, Hidde Burgmans, told the Guardian, “but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.”

items.title: The People Who Became Wildlife
items.summary:
W hat might it be like to be a bird? 

Initially Helen Lawy thought being a kestrel would mean freedom. “I love birds, and particularly kestrels — when they’re hovering, they have an amazing overview of the landscape,” she says. The kestrel’s extraordinarily flexible neck and head give it a sweeping view of the landscape, while its eyes can see ultraviolet light, which helps it detect the urine trails left by voles.  

“Immediately you’ve got a very different perspective,” Lawy says animatedly. 

Credit: Wayne Tuckwell / Shutterstock 
 A retired resident of Taunton, Lawy helps manage the 65-acre Longrun Meadow floodplain beside the River Tone in Somerset County, United Kingdom. When scientists asked for volunteers who wanted to attempt to view the landscape through an animal’s perspective, Lawy signed up and chose the reddish-brown kestrel, a small falcon. 

First she learned about the bird’s capabilities and habits. Then, over a period of several weeks, Lawy would spend hours sitting at the river’s edge and following the instructions of the “Animal Collaboration” guidebook she’d received: Sit still, pay attention, choose one sense that particularly matters to the animal. Because of the kestrels’ keen eyesight, Lawy would start with focusing on visual clues, then listen intently. “You become sort of hypervigilant,” she says.
